records.title: feat(compiler-world): add interface-aware reverse invalidation and world lifecycle proof
records.body:
Parent: #2425 / #2559
Depends on immutable compiler world: #8797
Public compile-interface authority: #5241
Semantic freshness/invalidation authority: #4241
Accepted workspace generation: #8642
Provider port/currentness: #4799, #6819
Cache/performance consumers: #2462, #5216
Representative journeys: #4245

## One-PR outcome

Derive deterministic reverse dependencies from the accepted compiler world, classify module/world transitions through #5241 public interfaces, invalidate exactly the required closure through #4241, and prove edit/delete/rename/root/configuration/SCC lifecycle behavior. This PR closes the initial #2425 compiler-world substrate; it does not promote a new provider fact class or implement persistent cache storage.

## Problem

An immutable world can still return stale cross-file facts unless each accepted transition identifies what changed, which modules/fact classes depend on it, and whether downstream compiler/provider artifacts remain reusable. Full-workspace invalidation would be correct but defeats the compiler programme; optimistic reuse without complete interface/dependency evidence is unsafe.

## Objective

Implement:

```text
accepted CompilerWorldSnapshot N
+ accepted WorkspaceSnapshot / CompilerWorldSnapshot N+1
+ #5241 module compile-interface transitions
→ typed WorldTransition
→ deterministic reverse dependency closure by phase/fact class
→ #4241 invalidation/currentness decisions
→ accepted current world/provider/cache eligibility
```

Private implementation changes may preserve downstream artifacts only when complete keys/interfaces prove no externally visible effect. Unknown or partial evidence invalidates conservatively with a typed reason.

## Dependency model

Build reverse adjacency from #8769/#8797 canonical graph identities. Retain dependency dimensions sufficient to decide impact:

- compile-time versus runtime-only edges;
- import/export/prototype/constant relationships;
- inheritance/role/composition;
- feature/version/pragma/include/environment contracts;
- package/stash/typeglob/dynamic boundary impact;
- generated/framework public members;
- SCC membership and schedule;
- source tier, root, configuration, and environment;
- provider/fact/artifact classes depending on each edge/interface component.

Do not create another module graph or interface digest. Consume #8769 topology and #5241 normalized transition authority.

## Transition classes

Distinguish at least:

```text
no semantic/world change
private implementation change
public declaration change
prototype/constant/import/export change
inheritance/composition/generated-member change
feature/version/pragma/environment/include change
compile-time edge change
runtime-only edge change
SCC membership/schedule change
dynamic-boundary widening or retirement
module/source rename, delete, re-add, or root movement
schema/profile/compiler change
partial/unknown/instrument failure
```

One transition may carry several dimensions. Missing interface/dependency evidence is conservative invalidation, not “unchanged.”

## Invalidation contract

- Compute deterministic affected module/SCC/fact/artifact/provider classes.
- Preserve owning-module implementation artifacts separately from downstream interface consumers.
- A private body edit with unchanged complete interface must not invalidate unrelated downstream modules.
- Public interface, compile-time edge, inheritance, environment, schema/profile, and SCC transitions invalidate the exact reverse closure.
- Runtime-only edge changes do not invalidate compile-time facts unless a declared consumer depends on them.
- Dynamic-boundary widening invalidates any prior exact facts that relied on the narrowed state.
- Dynamic-boundary retirement permits stronger facts only after ordinary current recomputation/proof; it does not resurrect old cache entries automatically.
- Delete/rename/root removal tombstones old identities before admitting replacements.
- Multi-root same-name modules remain isolated.
- Provider/cache eligibility records the exact world generation and invalidation decision; presence of a cached fact never establishes currentness.

## Lifecycle proof matrix

Use deterministic barriers and exact process/project fixtures for:

1. private body edit with stable interface;
2. public sub add/remove/rename;
3. prototype and constant change;
4. export/import/tag change;
5. parent/role/generated member change;
6. `use lib`/environment/configuration/root change;
7. add/remove compile-time edge;
8. runtime-only `require` change;
9. edit inside stable SCC;
10. SCC merge/split/schedule movement;
11. dynamic boundary widen/retire;
12. module delete/rename/re-add;
13. source-identical later generation;
14. held invalidation from N after N+1/N+2 publish;
15. cancellation, budget, and instrument failure;
16. shutdown/root removal cleanup.

Compare current results with an independent cold rebuild in tests. The cold oracle must not run in production or be hidden in performance receipts.

records.title: Datalog et graph queries — l'alternative SQL méconnue
records.body:
---
lede: Datalog est un langage de query déclaratif qui excelle là où SQL souffre : relations récursives, transitive closure, graph traversal. XTDB, Datomic, Datascript le rendent accessible.
lede_en: Datalog is a declarative query language excelling where SQL struggles: recursive relations, transitive closure, graph traversal. XTDB, Datomic, Datascript make it accessible.
title_en: Datalog and graph queries — the underrated SQL alternative
---

<!--lang:fr-->

## Pourquoi connaître Datalog

SQL est puissant mais souffre sur certaines requêtes :

- **Transitive closure** (qui est ancêtre de qui, qui suit qui directement ou indirectement) : nécessite `WITH RECURSIVE` complexe.
- **Graph traversal** : multi-hops, friend-of-friend, shortest path — SQL devient illisible.
- **Time-travel queries** : "qui était assigné à ce ticket il y a 3 mois ?" — partition par date manuelle.

Datalog résout ces cas naturellement, avec une syntaxe déclarative plus simple.

## Le concept

Datalog s'inspire de Prolog. Vous écrivez des **règles** (faits + dérivations) et des **queries**.

```clojure
;; Datalog (syntaxe EDN, Datomic-style)
;; Trouver tous les ancêtres de Khalil

[:find ?ancestor
 :where
 [?khalil :person/name "Khalil"]
 [?khalil :person/parent ?ancestor]]

;; Récursif : tous les ancêtres directs et indirects
[:find ?ancestor
 :where
 [?khalil :person/name "Khalil"]
 (ancestor ?khalil ?ancestor)]

;; Rule definition
(rule ancestor [?person ?ancestor]
  ((or [?person :person/parent ?ancestor]
       (and [?person :person/parent ?intermediate]
            (ancestor ?intermediate ?ancestor)))))
```

La rule récursive est triviale. En SQL, vous écrivez du `WITH RECURSIVE` de 20 lignes.

## Where it excels

- **Recursive queries** : ancêtres, descendants, hierarchies illimitées.
- **Graph patterns** : matching de sous-graphes complexes.
- **Transitive relations** : "tous les users connectés à X par n'importe quelle chaîne d'amitiés".
- **Audit / time-travel** : Datomic stocke immutable history, queries "as of t" naturelles.

## Les implémentations modernes

**XTDB** :

- Open source, écrit en Clojure.
- Time-travel queries natives.
- Pluggable storage (RocksDB, Kafka, JDBC).
- API HTTP standard.

**Datomic** :

- Commercial (Cognitect, Nubank).
- Production-grade, utilisé par Walmart, plusieurs banques.
- Modèle économique : queries gratuites (sur peer JVM), writes payants.

**Datascript** :

- Datalog dans le navigateur (ClojureScript).
- État local d'apps React-like reactive en datalog.
- Sweet spot : Roam Research, Logseq.

**Datalevin** :

- Open source, embedded, écrit en Clojure.
- Alternative à SQLite pour des apps avec relations complexes.

## Cas d'usage 2026

- **Knowledge graphs** : Roam Research, Logseq, Obsidian — tous datalog underneath.
- **Apps d'analyse réseau** : qui est connecté à qui, influencer maps.
- **Génétique / biotechnologie** : relations dans des graphes biologiques.
- **Compliance & audit** : "qui a touché à ce record et quand ?" — datalog time-travel.

## Vs Cypher (Neo4j)

Neo4j utilise **Cypher**, un autre langage de graph query. Différences :

- **Cypher** : optimisé pour les graphes, ASCII-art syntax pour les paths.
- **Datalog** : plus général, peut aussi faire du relationnel pur.

```cypher
// Cypher
MATCH (k:Person {name: 'Khalil'})-[:PARENT*]->(ancestor)
RETURN ancestor
```

Cypher reste plus populaire pour graph databases pures. Datalog brille pour les apps mixant relationnel + graph + history.

## Limites

- **Talent pool** : encore plus restreint que SQL. Recrutement difficile.
- **Tooling** : SQL a 50 ans d'écosystème. Datalog a moins de tutoriels, moins d'IDE support.
- **Performance** : sur des queries simples, SQL souvent plus rapide grâce à des décennies d'optimisations.

## Apprendre Datalog

- **Learn Datalog Today** (gratuit en ligne) : cours interactif court.
- **Datascript playground** : essayer dans le browser.
- **Building a Datomic app** tutoriels.

Apprendre Datalog en 1 weekend rend meilleur en SQL aussi — vous comprenez différemment les relations.

## Verdict

Pour 95 % des projets : SQL reste le bon choix. Pour des apps spécifiques avec graph traversal, time-travel, ou knowledge management : Datalog mérite un essai.

Comme Common Lisp : pas mainstream, mais ceux qui l'utilisent ne reviennent rarement à SQL pur. Investissement intellectuel qui paye.

SQL is powerful but suffers on some queries:

Datalog handles these naturally, with a simpler declarative syntax.

**RCV-DIRECT — one direct accepted callable/accessor-result receiver transition.**

```text

THIS ISSUE

#7438 direct accessor-result completion
```

Extend the canonical #9472 receiver query so one complete/current #10787 `MaterializedCallResult` may become one exact receiver when the result contains exactly one admitted current object/package alternative.

```text
SemanticQueryOutcome<MaterializedCallResult>
```

from #10787 and return `Exact(PackageIdentity)` only when:

- the outcome is complete and current for one accepted snapshot;

```text
one exact object alternative     → Exact(receiver)

bare/void/non-object              → no exact receiver
```

A method name existing on one candidate cannot restore exactness.

Every success or boundary retains:

```text

receiver/argument/context input identity
#10787 query and accepted snapshot identity
CallableResultFact and materialization identity
per-alternative origin/evidence identity

caller/callee/document/root/project/profile generations
source tier + edit authority
producer/proof/confidence/completeness/limitations

```

Do not retain only a package string, display name, URI/range, or result-global anchor list.

## Currentness and invalidation

Exercise independently:

- caller receiver, argument, target, or context edit;
- callee-only return/relation/evidence edit with unchanged caller bytes;
- close/reopen caller or callee;
- delete/re-add callee;

- accepted snapshot/profile/source-tier change;
- held generation N released after N+1 acceptance.

Old exact receiver output becomes ineligible before replacement exact output. The query consumes #10787 currentness and introduces no second result cache

records.title: [discussion] MPTT Replacement
records.body:
On the anniversary of our [previous major tree structure change](https://github.com/inventree/InvenTree/pull/9979):

# Concurrency Issues with MPTT

## Background

InvenTree uses [django-mptt](https://github.com/django-mptt/django-mptt) to manage tree structures for five models:

| Model | Tree relationship |
| --- | --- |
| `PartCategory` | Category hierarchy |
| `Part` | Variant hierarchy (`variant_of`) |
| `StockLocation` | Location hierarchy |
| `StockItem` | Stock item ancestry (splits / serialization) |
| `Build` | Parent / child build orders |

MPTT stores pre-computed `tree_id` / `lft` / `rght` / `level` values on every row. This makes subtree reads cheap, but every insert, move or delete must update many sibling / ancestor rows, which can prove expensive when updating a large number of items.

Additionally, the added row values can become inconsistent under concurrent writes. In production this manifests as recurring errors such as:

```
More than one root node with tree_id 32034. That's invalid, do a full rebuild.
```

raised from `rebuild_stock_item_tree` and `StockItem.partial_rebuild` - typically observed when consuming stock against large build orders while multiple users are active. The error occurs when a tree rebuild discovers that two root nodes (`parent = None`) share the same `tree_id`. The duplicate roots are created earlier, by unrelated concurrent operations (see bugs below), and every subsequent operation on the poisoned `tree_id` then fails until a full tree rebuild runs.

### Example Error Log

```python
Traceback (most recent call last):

  File "/opt/inventree/src/backend/InvenTree/InvenTree/models.py", line 958, in partial_rebuild
    self.__class__.objects.partial_rebuild(tree_id)

  File "/opt/inventree/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mptt/managers.py", line 46, in wrapped
    return method(self, *args, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

  File "/opt/inventree/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mptt/managers.py", line 716, in partial_rebuild
    raise RuntimeError(

RuntimeError: More than one root node with tree_id 32034. That's invalid, do a full rebuild.

```

## django-mptt is unmaintained

The django-mptt project explicitly declares itself unmaintained, and its README acknowledges this exact failure class:

> "every insert, move, or delete must update a potentially large number of sibling and ancestor rows. This write amplification is the fundamental reason the library is hard to maintain: **concurrent writes can race and corrupt the tree**, bulk operations bypass the update logic entirely, and any code that touches the database outside of django-mptt (raw SQL, `bulk_update`, migrations) can leave the tree in an inconsistent state."

## Bugs / weak spots identified in the current codebase

### 1. Racy `tree_id` allocation (`MAX + 1`, no locking)

Every `tree_id` allocator in the codebase (and inside django-mptt itself) is an unlocked read-then-write of `SELECT MAX(tree_id) + 1`:

- `InvenTreeTree.getNextTreeID()` (`src/backend/InvenTree/InvenTree/models.py`, ~L1006) - used when saving new root nodes and when reassigning subtrees during root deletion.
- `StockItem._create_serial_numbers()` (`src/backend/InvenTree/stock/models.py`, ~L712) - allocates an entire *range* of tree_ids in Python and `bulk_create`s root nodes into them. Called from three concurrent-user hot paths: build output creation (`build/models.py` ~L873), PO receipt of serialized stock (`order/models.py` ~L1199), and the stock serialization API (`stock/api.py` ~L1259).
- django-mptt's own `TreeManager._get_next_tree_id()` - same pattern, hit on any root insert that goes through `MPTTModel.save()`.

Two concurrent transactions read the same `MAX`, both insert root nodes at the same `tree_id`, and both commit cleanly. Two users simultaneously creating serialized build outputs / receiving purchase orders can corrupt dozens of tree_ids in a single race.

### 2. Concurrent MPTT writes corrupt `lft` / `rght`

Concurrent child inserts into the same tree (e.g. two users splitting stock from the same tree) interleave MPTT's space-making SQL, producing invalid interval values. The follow-up `partial_rebuild` normally heals this (it derives structure from parent links), but:

- Two concurrent rebuilds of the same tree interleave their bulk updates and leave garbage.
- `InvenTreeTree.delete()` computes subtree membership from `get_descendants()`, which *trusts* `lft`/`rght`. If run while the interval data is corrupt, promoted children can be missed during `tree_id` reassignment - converting transient interval noise into a persistent duplicate root.

### 3. The recovery path can re-corrupt data

On partial rebuild failure, a full `StockItem.objects.rebuild()` is offloaded to the background worker while web workers continue mutating stock. `rebuild()` renumbers **all** tree_ids and is itself unsafe against concurrent inserts.

### 4. No database-level guard

There is no constraint preventing two root

# Phase 3: First-Class Twin API

Milestone 3 — Ditto-Style Twin Layer. Roadmap phase 3 of 6.

## Goal
Twins become first-class resources: search, write, and graph navigation with embedded state.

## Requirement
- **R3 — Twin API primera clase**: `GET /api/twins` paginated search, attributes/features writes, graph expand with embedded state (tenant-scoped recursive CTEs), `relationsQuery` in REST, OpenAPI-first.

## Plans (3)
- [ ] **03-01 (Wave 1)** — Topology tenant-scoped traversal foundation + CTE benchmark (`NeighborsTenant`, dedup UNION, `ExpandWithCTE`, synthetic depth 5-10 benchmark fixing limits)
- [ ] **03-02 (Wave 2)** — Twin listing + graph expansion (read plane): `GET /api/twins` cursor pagination + filters; `?expand=relations(depth)` with embedded state
- [ ] **03-03 (Wave 3)** — Model-validated state writes + REST `relationsQuery`: `PUT/PATCH .../attributes|features` reusing the Phase 2 enforcer; `relationsQuery` in `/api/entitiesQuery`

records.title: Extend js: read-type conversion through positional-union wrappers (set-operation / raw recursive CTE) via cross-branch agreement
records.body:
## Summary

`#310` added an opt-in `js:` read type for `bigint` columns (`{ type: 'bigint', js: 'bigint' | 'number' }`),
converting values at the adapter read boundary via compiled-query column provenance (`columnMetadata`).

Conversion currently works for **plain `select` and `include`** queries. It does **not** yet flow through the
query wrappers that reconstruct a `CompiledQuery` without carrying `columnMetadata` forward:

- **Set operations** (`UNION` / `UNION ALL` / `INTERSECT` / `EXCEPT`) — `compileSetOperation` /
  `compileLeafOrBranch` return only `{ sql, parameters }`.
- **CTE-wrapped selects** — the outer compile drops the inner select's metadata.
- **Recursive CTEs** — the recursive compiler and the core recursive execution path rebuild a metadata-less query.

As of `#310`, these paths **fail loud**: a query on one of these shapes whose output carries a `js:` column
throws a clear error (`js read type not yet supported through <set-operation|CTE|recursive CTE>; use a plain
select`) instead of silently returning the raw string. This preserves the project's "never silently weaker"
tenet — the gap is closed *safely*, not hidden.

## Task

Thread `columnMetadata` through the wrapper paths so `js:` read conversion works for set operations, CTEs, and
recursive CTEs, then remove the fail-loud guards.

### Correct model: provenance is a property of the RESOLVED OUTPUT SCHEMA, not of any single leaf

`js:` read intent must be computed from the set operation's resolved output schema — the same schema SQL itself
defines by unifying **all** branches positionally (union-compatibility + type unification). The output column
*names* come from the first query, but the column *identity/intent* at position `i` is only well-defined by the
**agreement of every branch** at `i`. Basing conversion on the first leaf alone ignores the other branches and
would apply (e.g.) `js:'bigint'` to values contributed by a different, non-`js:` column in another branch (a
plain `text`/counter column) — the exact provenance bug class as the batch-values finding. Type-compatibility
(`int8` ≈ `int8`) does not imply same read intent.

**Required rule (cross-branch agreement fold):** the set-op's output `columnMetadata` for position `i` = the
`js:` setting shared by **all** branches at `i`; if the branches disagree or any branch at `i` is not a `js:`
column, output column `i` carries **no** `js:` → do not convert. This is strictly better than a blanket throw:
it converts when all branches agree (the common `UNION` of same-shape rows) and simply abstains otherwise — no
error needed. The work is this fold over the resolved schema, NOT copying one leaf's metadata.

- **CTE / recursive CTE: single-source is covered; positional unions are NOT.** A simple CTE and a
  traversal-based recursive CTE (whose base and step both project the same node table at the same positions)
  are single-source — the inner select's `columnMetadata` carries through unambiguously, and this is already
  covered. But a **raw recursive CTE** (`buildRawCte`, arbitrary base + step query builders) is a positional
  `base UNION step` with the SAME cross-branch problem as set operations: the step branch may project a
  computed expression or a different source column at a given position, so applying the base branch's `js`
  metadata to the merged column is wrong. As of the #310 follow-up it **fails loud** (like set operations)
  rather than silently applying base metadata; covering it requires the same cross-branch agreement fold as
  set operations — tracked here.
- **CTE-name shadowing (fail-closed, fixed in #310, not deferred):** a `RangeVar` whose name matches a `WITH`
  CTE is never resolved as a model table (it would build metadata for the base table while SQL reads the CTE).
  This is a correctness fix, not part of the deferred cross-branch work.
- Estimated ~120–200 prod LOC + tests across `set-operation.ts`, `adapter-compiler-recursive.ts`,
  `pgsql-adapter.ts`, and `recursive-query-builder.ts`.

## Acceptance

- A `UNION` / CTE / recursive query selecting a `js:'bigint'` (and `js:'number'`) column returns converted
  values (BigInt / range-checked number), matching plain-select behavior.
- The fail-loud guards are removed once coverage lands.
- e2e coverage for each shape (real PostgreSQL).

records.title: Implement directory-aware copy and move with recursive progress and verification
records.body:
## Problem

Copy and move operations must handle directories as first-class items. A two-panel file manager should allow users to copy or move selected folders with the same reliability guarantees as single files.

Current risk: if the UI path treats selected items as files only, folder operations can be incomplete, unsupported, or inconsistent with the app's safety promise.

## Desired behavior

Copying or moving a directory should recursively process its contents, preserve the directory structure, verify copied file contents, and report progress at both item and total-operation level.

## Scope

- Detect when selected items are directories.
- Route directories through recursive copy/move logic instead of file-only copy/move.
- Create destination directories as needed.
- Traverse nested directories safely.
- Verify copied files according to the current checksum settings.
- Track total files, total bytes, current file, completed files, and failed files.
- Prevent infinite recursion caused by symlinks, aliases, or directory cycles.
- Keep move semantics safe: delete source only after copy and verification succeed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Copying a selected folder copies all nested files and subfolders.
- [ ] Moving a selected folder does not remove the source unless the destination copy and verification succeed.
- [ ] Recursive progress is visible to the user.
- [ ] Partial failures are reported with per-file errors.
- [ ] Directory cycles and symlink loops do not hang the app.
- [ ] Unit tests cover nested directories, empty directories, mixed file/folder selections, and failure cases.

## Implementation notes

Relevant areas:

- `OtterTwin/Views/MainView.swift`
- `OtterTwin/Services/FileOperationService.swift`
- `OtterTwin/VFS/VFSProvider.swift`
- `OtterTwin/VFS/LocalProvider.swift`

Consider introducing an operation planner that expands a selection into a list/tree of file operations before execution.

## Non-goals

- Full operation queue.
- Resume after crash.
- Metadata preservation beyond what current providers already support.

records.title: Unbounded recursion in type and module closures: self-referential :<, unbound supertype variable, mutual imports
records.body:
Version: `metta-repl 0.2.10`, checkout `3f76dc460da6961f57f69f6c3e550c59c74ada83`. Each reproducer was run as its own file under `( ulimit -v 4194304; timeout 30 metta-repl <file> )` so the failure mode is observable as an exit code rather than a lost machine.

Three reproducers, one shape: a recursive closure computation with no bound.

1. **Self-referential subtype declaration.** `!(add-atom &self (:< (F $x) (F (F $x))))` followed by any typed query: `add_super_types` (`lib/src/metta/types.rs:49-62`) recurses whenever a round appended anything, with no depth or size bound. Killed at 30 s, exit 124, nothing printed. Structural subtyping with recursive constructors is undecidable in general, so a bound-and-report or a decidable fragment are the published outs; the declaration passes both well-formedness checks, so validation cannot exclude it today.

2. **Unbound supertype variable.** A `(:< A $z)` whose supertype side carries a variable the subtype side never binds: stack overflow, exit 134, no result at all.

3. **Mutual module imports.** Two modules that import each other: the alternating module path keeps extending until the guard kills the process, exit 124.

Could the three closures carry a bound (rounds, depth, or a visited set) and report the truncation as an error result rather than hanging or exhausting the stack?

records.title: shortest_path() has no edge_types filter, unlike expand()/traverse()

## Summary

`graph.shortest_path()` and `graph.weighted_shortest_path()` take no `edge_types` argument, while `graph.expand()` and `graph.traverse()` do. There is no way to restrict a shortest path to a subset of relationship types.

```sql
graph.shortest_path(
  source_table regclass,
  source_id text,
  target_table regclass,
  target_id text,
  max_depth int DEFAULT 20,
  hydrate boolean DEFAULT true
)
```

## Why it matters

Relationship-typed shortest path is the common shape of the query. "How is this chunk connected to that chunk *through shared entities*" is a different question from "how is it connected through any edge", and only the first is usually meaningful.

The current workaround is to register and build a second property graph containing only the wanted edge types, then `select_graph()` before querying. That works, but:

- On a 1.29M node / 3.2M edge graph the restricted build took **~55 s** (`build_graph()` → `nodes_loaded=1288553 edges_loaded=3199812 build_time_ms=54611`).
- It produces a second on-disk artifact and a second in-memory projection, so the cost is per relationship-type combination rather than per query.
- With `max_loaded_graphs_per_backend = 1`, alternating between the full graph and the restricted graph inside one backend causes unload/reload, so callers need connection pinning to avoid it.

## How I hit it

I was comparing `shortest_path()` against a hand-written recursive CTE on the same tables. My graph had two edge types (`m_chunk`/`m_entity` from a junction table, plus `has_chunk`). Without edge-type restriction the two engines were answering different questions — `shortest_path()` was routing through `has_chunk`, producing shorter paths than the MENTIONS-only CTE. Path lengths disagreed on 6 of 6 sampled pairs until I rebuilt a MENTIONS-only graph, after which they matched exactly on all 6.

That is a correctness trap for anyone benchmarking or cross-checking `shortest_path()` against another engine, since nothing in the signature signals that all edge types participate.

## Request

Add `edge_types text[] DEFAULT NULL` to `shortest_path()` and `weighted_shortest_path()`, with the same semantics as in `expand()`/`traverse()` (NULL = all types). This would also remove the need for per-type graph registration in the common case.

If restricting inside the CSR traversal is not straightforward, even documenting the current behavior in `api-reference.mdx` — "all registered edge types participate; register a separate graph to restrict" — would prevent the mismatch above.

## Environment

`ghcr.io/evokoa/pggraph:1.0.0`, PostgreSQL 17.10, linux/arm64.
